6754.etyen:
PIE word
 *bʰúHt
Inherited from Old Norse búð (“dwelling; booth, temporary hut”), a variant of Old Norse bóð, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building, hut; dwelling”), a nominal derivative of Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell, reside”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk bu (“hut, shed”), Icelandic búð, Faroese búð, Swedish bod, Danish bod, German Bude and English booth (“booth, hut; small shop”). / PIE word
 *bʰúHt
Borrowed from Danish bod (“booth, stall; shop”), from Old Danish bōð (“booth, stall”), from Old East Norse bóð (“booth, dwelling”), from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building, hut; dwelling”), a nominal derivative of Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell, reside”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”).
Compare Swedish bod, German Bude and English booth (“booth, stall; small shop”). / Probably shortened from haugbu (“wight dwelling in a burial mound”), from Old Norse haugbúi (“dweller in a burial mound”). The second element is Old Norse búi (“dweller, inhabitant; farmer”), from Proto-Germanic *būô (“dweller, inhabitant”), ultimately related to the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”).
Compare the related inhabitant-forming elements Norwegian Nynorsk -bu, Swedish -bo and Danish -bo (“inhabitant of a place”).

Internationalism, based on Latin Armenia, from Ancient Greek Ἀρμενία (Armenía), from Old Persian 𐎠𐎼𐎷𐎡𐎴 (a-r-mi-i-n, “Armenia”). The Old Persian form Armina is first attested around 520 BCE in the Behistun Inscription of Darius I, where it denotes an Achaemenid province; the corresponding Babylonian version instead uses the older regional name Urartu. The related Old Persian form Arminiya- denoted an Armenian or inhabitant of the province.

1000546.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Latin Neptūnus (“Neptune, the Roman god of water and the sea”). The Norwegian form reflects the widespread international form of the name without the Latin ending -us.
The deeper origin of the Latin name is disputed. One proposal derives Neptūnus from Proto-Italic *neptūnos, ultimately connecting it with Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud, moisture, mist”) and a notion of wetness or moisture. 1001314.etyen:
A Norwegian variant of Emilia, ultimately from Latin Aemilia (“female given name”), the feminine form of the Roman nomen Aemilius. The Latin name is traditionally connected with aemulus (“eager; emulating, rivaling”). The spelling may also reflect French Émilie, and the name may alternatively be understood as a feminine derivative of Emil.
Compare Danish Emilie, Swedish Emilie, German Emilie, French Émilie and English Emily.
